claim: Expansion microscopy (ExM) circumvents the diffraction limit of light microscopy by physically expanding the specimen four-fold in each dimension.
source: Expansion microscopy (ExM) circumvents the diffraction limit of light microscopy by physically expanding the specimen four-fold in each dimension (Chen et al., 2015; Tillberg et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Tillberg et al., 2016.

claim: Expansion is achieved by chemically anchoring proteins and other biomolecules directly to a hyper-swelling gel, followed by aggressive proteolysis to enable uniform swelling of the gel material.
source: Expansion is achieved by chemically anchoring proteins and other biomolecules directly to a hyper-swelling gel, followed by aggressive proteolysis to enable uniform swelling of the gel material.
evidence: This describes the established ExM methodology based on scientific knowledge of the technique.

claim: Other super-resolution approaches are not readily compatible with thick tissue slices and require specialized optics.
source: While other super-resolution approaches are not readily compatible with thick tissue slices and require specialized optics (Hell and Wichmann, 1994), fluorophores (Rust et al., 2006), or software (Gustafsson, 2000), ExM is compatible with any microscope (Gao et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016), including other super-resolution modalities (Gao et al., 2018; Halpern et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2019), and performs well in both cultured cells and thick tissue slices (Chen et al., 2015; Tillberg et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Hell and Wichmann, 1994; Rust et al., 2006; and Gustafsson, 2000.

claim: ExM is compatible with any microscope, including other super-resolution modalities.
source: While other super-resolution approaches are not readily compatible with thick tissue slices and require specialized optics (Hell and Wichmann, 1994), fluorophores (Rust et al., 2006), or software (Gustafsson, 2000), ExM is compatible with any microscope (Gao et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016), including other super-resolution modalities (Gao et al., 2018; Halpern et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2019), and performs well in both cultured cells and thick tissue slices (Chen et al., 2015; Tillberg et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2018; Halpern et al., 2017; and Xu et al., 2019.

claim: ExM performs well in both cultured cells and thick tissue slices.
source: While other super-resolution approaches are not readily compatible with thick tissue slices and require specialized optics (Hell and Wichmann, 1994), fluorophores (Rust et al., 2006), or software (Gustafsson, 2000), ExM is compatible with any microscope (Gao et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016), including other super-resolution modalities (Gao et al., 2018; Halpern et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2019), and performs well in both cultured cells and thick tissue slices (Chen et al., 2015; Tillberg et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Tillberg et al., 2016.

claim: The resolution increase of ExM depends on the expansion factor of the gel recipe used, assuming sufficiently high labeling density.
source: Assuming sufficiently high labeling density, the resolution increase of ExM depends on the expansion factor of the gel recipe used.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the principle that physical expansion increases resolution proportionally.

claim: Iterative ExM (iExM) uses sequential embedding in multiple expansion gels to achieve 15× and greater expansion.
source: For example, iterative ExM (iExM) uses sequential embedding in multiple expansion gels to achieve 15× and greater expansion but requires a complex sequence of gel re-embedding, link cleaving, and fluorophore transfer (Chang et al., 2017), limiting its broad adoption.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2017.

claim: iExM requires a complex sequence of gel re-embedding, link cleaving, and fluorophore transfer, limiting its broad adoption.
source: For example, iterative ExM (iExM) uses sequential embedding in multiple expansion gels to achieve 15× and greater expansion but requires a complex sequence of gel re-embedding, link cleaving, and fluorophore transfer (Chang et al., 2017), limiting its broad adoption.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2017 and inference about adoption barriers.

claim: The expansion factor of the gel can be improved by decreasing the concentration of crosslinker, usually bisacrylamide (bis).
source: The expansion factor of the gel itself can be improved by decreasing the concentration of crosslinker (Okay, 2009), usually bisacrylamide (bis), although this is generally at the expense of the mechanical integrity of the gel.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Okay, 2009.

claim: Decreasing crosslinker concentration is generally at the expense of the mechanical integrity of the gel.
source: The expansion factor of the gel itself can be improved by decreasing the concentration of crosslinker (Okay, 2009), usually bisacrylamide (bis), although this is generally at the expense of the mechanical integrity of the gel.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Okay, 2009 and general knowledge of polymer chemistry.

claim: Reducing the bis concentration in the original ExM recipe from 1.5 to 0.25 mg/mL produces an approximately nine-fold expanding gel.
source: For example, reducing the bis concentration in the original ExM recipe from 1.5 to 0.25 mg/mL produces an approximately nine-fold expanding gel (Chen et al., 2015, SF5), but these gels are too soft to hold their shape under the force of gravity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015, SF5.

claim: Gels with bis concentration reduced to 0.25 mg/mL are too soft to hold their shape under the force of gravity.
source: For example, reducing the bis concentration in the original ExM recipe from 1.5 to 0.25 mg/mL produces an approximately nine-fold expanding gel (Chen et al., 2015, SF5), but these gels are too soft to hold their shape under the force of gravity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015, SF5.

claim: Low-crosslinker gels are difficult to handle without breaking and display nonuniform expansion.
source: As a result, they are difficult to handle without breaking and display nonuniform expansion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanical properties described for low-crosslinker gels.

claim: The tradeoff of expansion versus gel mechanical integrity has not been explored in a quantitative or systematic way.
source: This tradeoff of expansion versus gel mechanical integrity has not been explored in a quantitative or systematic way.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: A gel recipe variant using a high concentration of the monomer dimethylacrylamide (DMAA) has enough crosslinking through side reactions and polymer chain entanglement that the crosslinker can be omitted entirely, producing ~10-fold expansion in one step.
source: Another gel recipe variant, using a high concentration of the monomer dimethylacrylamide (DMAA), has enough crosslinking through side reactions and polymer chain entanglement that the crosslinker can be omitted entirely, producing ~10-fold expansion in one step (Truckenbrodt et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Truckenbrodt et al., 2018.

claim: The DMAA-based recipe has been used to expand cultured cells and thin cryosectioned tissue.
source: This recipe has been used to expand cultured cells and thin cryosectioned tissue (Truckenbrodt et al., 2019), but reportedly requires rigorous degassing to remove oxygen prior to gelation, making it laborious to use.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Truckenbrodt et al., 2019.

claim: The DMAA-based recipe reportedly requires rigorous degassing to remove oxygen prior to gelation, making it laborious to use.
source: This recipe has been used to expand cultured cells and thin cryosectioned tissue (Truckenbrodt et al., 2019), but reportedly requires rigorous degassing to remove oxygen prior to gelation, making it laborious to use.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Truckenbrodt et al., 2019 and inference about labor requirements.

claim: Expansion of thick tissue slices (>50 µm) has not been demonstrated using the DMAA-based method.
source: Moreover, expansion of thick tissue slices (>50 µm) has not been demonstrated using this method.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior work based on literature review.

claim: A robustly validated and easily adoptable method that is compatible with multiple sample types and enables single-step expansion well over 4× without compromising gel integrity is lacking.
source: Thus, a robustly validated and easily adoptable method that is compatible with multiple sample types and enables single-step expansion well over 4× without compromising gel integrity is lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the field that motivates the current work.

claim: The authors explored the expansion gel recipe space in a systematic manner, assessing the limits of single-round expansion using reagents and methods familiar to labs already performing ExM.
source: Here, we explored the expansion gel recipe space in a systematic manner, assessing the limits of single-round expansion using reagents and methods that would be familiar to labs already performing ExM.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the manuscript.

claim: For any given choice of recipe parameters, varying the crosslinker alone yielded a family of recipes whose expansion factor and mechanical quality vary smoothly from high-expanding, mechanically unstable to low-expanding, tough gels.
source: For any given choice of recipe parameters (monomer concentrations, gelation temperature, initiator concentration, etc.), varying the crosslinker alone yielded a family of recipes whose expansion factor and mechanical quality vary smoothly from high-expanding, mechanically unstable to low-expanding, tough gels.
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic exploration described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1.

claim: A range of crosslinker concentrations was tested for each family because the optimal crosslinker concentration may vary by family.
source: A range of crosslinker concentrations was tested for each family because the optimal crosslinker concentration may vary by family.
evidence: This explains the experimental design rationale.

claim: TREx is an optimized ExM method that allows for robust 10-fold expansion in a single step.
source: From this exploration, we generated Ten-fold Robust Expansion Microscopy (TREx), an optimized ExM method that allows for robust 10-fold expansion in a single step.
evidence: This is the main claim of the manuscript, supported by the data presented throughout.

claim: TREx can be used to expand both thick tissue slices and adherent cells.
source: We show that TREx can be used to expand both thick tissue slices and adherent cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2-5.

claim: TREx is compatible with antibodies and off-the-shelf small-molecule stains for total protein and membranes.
source: It is compatible with antibodies and off-the-shelf small-molecule stains for total protein and membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2-5.

claim: TREx enables 3D nanoscopic imaging of specific structures stained with antibodies in combination with cellular ultrastructure.
source: Together, we show that TREx enables 3D nanoscopic imaging of specific structures stained with antibodies in combination with cellular ultrastructure.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2-5.

claim: Reducing the crosslinker to 300 µg/mL in the original ExM recipe increased the expansion to ~9×.
source: Consistent with Chen et al., 2015, reducing the crosslinker to 300 µg/mL increased the expansion to ~9×, below which the gels fail to form consistently (Figure 1B, purple).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015 and data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Below 300 µg/mL crosslinker, gels from the original ExM recipe family fail to form consistently.
source: Consistent with Chen et al., 2015, reducing the crosslinker to 300 µg/mL increased the expansion to ~9×, below which the gels fail to form consistently (Figure 1B, purple).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The high-monomer recipe family (family B) was inspired by the 4×-expanding Ultra-ExM recipe from Gambarotto et al., 2019.
source: We next characterized a high-monomer recipe family (family B) inspired by the 4×-expanding Ultra-ExM recipe from Gambarotto et al., 2019, which found that a higher monomer concentration relative to the original ExM recipe was necessary for high-fidelity preservation of the shape of centrioles.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gambarotto et al., 2019.

claim: A higher monomer concentration relative to the original ExM recipe was necessary for high-fidelity preservation of the shape of centrioles.
source: We next characterized a high-monomer recipe family (family B) inspired by the 4×-expanding Ultra-ExM recipe from Gambarotto et al., 2019, which found that a higher monomer concentration relative to the original ExM recipe was necessary for high-fidelity preservation of the shape of centrioles.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gambarotto et al., 2019.

claim: For the high-monomer family of recipes, expansion as a function of crosslinker concentration was shifted leftward compared to standard ExM.
source: Indeed, for this high-monomer family of recipes, expansion as a function of crosslinker concentration was shifted leftward compared to standard ExM (Figure 1B, blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: As the crosslinker was decreased below 30 µg/mL in family B, the increase in expansion factor saturated around 11.5×.
source: As the crosslinker was decreased below 30 µg/mL, the increase in expansion factor saturated around 11.5×.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: For a given expansion factor, the high-monomer gel holds its shape better than the corresponding standard ExM gel.
source: The deformation index versus expansion factor curve for the high-monomer family ran below that for standard ExM, indicating that for a given expansion factor the high-monomer gel holds its shape better than the corresponding standard ExM gel (Figure 1D, blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The high-monomer family uses a higher concentration of radical initiator and accelerator to trigger polymerization compared to standard ExM (5 mg/mL each of APS and TEMED, versus 2 mg/mL in standard ExM).
source: Compared with standard ExM, this high-monomer family uses a higher concentration of radical initiator and accelerator to trigger polymerization (5 mg/mL each of APS and TEMED, versus 2 mg/mL in standard ExM).
evidence: This describes the recipe composition as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The high initiation rate of family B causes gels to form within minutes at room temperature.
source: We found that this high initiation rate causes gels to form within minutes at room temperature (RT).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: The rates of initiation and polymerization increase with temperature.
source: Because the rates of initiation and polymerization increase with temperature, it is likely that specimens are not fully equilibrating to the gelation temperature of 37°C before the onset of gelation, introducing a potential source of experimental variability.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of polymer chemistry.

claim: Specimens are likely not fully equilibrating to the gelation temperature of 37°C before the onset of gelation in family B, introducing a potential source of experimental variability.
source: Because the rates of initiation and polymerization increase with temperature, it is likely that specimens are not fully equilibrating to the gelation temperature of 37°C before the onset of gelation, introducing a potential source of experimental variability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid gelation observed.

claim: Rapid gelation makes the gelation chamber assembly step more time sensitive.
source: This rapid gelation makes the gelation chamber assembly step more time sensitive and presents challenges for adapting the technique to thick tissue slices as thick tissue slices require extra time for the gelation solution to diffuse throughout the sample prior to polymerization.
evidence: This is an inference about practical implications of rapid gelation.

claim: Thick tissue slices require extra time for the gelation solution to diffuse throughout the sample prior to polymerization.
source: This rapid gelation makes the gelation chamber assembly step more time sensitive and presents challenges for adapting the technique to thick tissue slices as thick tissue slices require extra time for the gelation solution to diffuse throughout the sample prior to polymerization.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of diffusion processes in biological samples.

claim: The expansion versus crosslinker curve for family C was similar to family B for high crosslinker concentrations but displayed a slightly greater slope.
source: The expansion versus crosslinker curve for this family was similar to family B for high crosslinker concentrations but displayed a slightly greater slope.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Unlike family B, the expansion factor of family C did not saturate upon decreasing the crosslinker concentration.
source: Unlike family B, the expansion factor did not saturate upon decreasing the crosslinker concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The expansion factor of family C continued to increase to 13× expansion at 10 µg/mL crosslinker.
source: Instead, the expansion factor continued to increase to 13× expansion at 10 µg/mL crosslinker (Figure 1B, red), with zero-crosslinker gels failing to form.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Zero-crosslinker gels in family C failed to form.
source: Instead, the expansion factor continued to increase to 13× expansion at 10 µg/mL crosslinker (Figure 1B, red), with zero-crosslinker gels failing to form.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Family C enables 10-fold expansion without sacrificing acceptable gel mechanical quality at 30 µg/mL bis.
source: Family C enables 10-fold expansion without sacrificing acceptable gel mechanical quality (30 µg/mL bis, Figure 1D, red), and without the faster, less controlled gelation kinetics of family B.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Family C does not have the faster, less controlled gelation kinetics of family B.
source: Family C enables 10-fold expansion without sacrificing acceptable gel mechanical quality (30 µg/mL bis, Figure 1D, red), and without the faster, less controlled gelation kinetics of family B.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lower initiator concentration in family C.

claim: Recipe families B and C feature a high fraction of sodium acrylate relative to acrylamide.
source: The recipe families explored above (B, C) feature a high fraction of sodium acrylate relative to acrylamide.
evidence: This describes the composition of the recipes as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Acrylate drives expansion of the gel.
source: Acrylate drives expansion of the gel but comes in widely varying purity levels and, in some cases, causes tissue to shrink.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of polymer chemistry and ExM methodology.

claim: Acrylate comes in widely varying purity levels and, in some cases, causes tissue to shrink.
source: Acrylate drives expansion of the gel but comes in widely varying purity levels and, in some cases, causes tissue to shrink.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of reagent properties and potential artifacts.

claim: Macroscopic tissue shrinkage from acrylate is modest compared to the gel expansion but may not be uniform at all scales.
source: This macroscopic tissue shrinkage is modest compared to the gel expansion but may not be uniform at all scales.
evidence: This is speculation about potential non-uniformity of shrinkage effects.

claim: Recipe family D has a higher acrylamide to acrylate ratio (2.1:1) compared to families B and C.
source: We therefore tested an alternative recipe family (D) with higher acrylamide to acrylate ratio (2.1:1).
evidence: This describes the composition of recipe family D as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Increasing the acrylamide to acrylate ratio did not change the expansion factors appreciably at a given crosslinker concentration.
source: Increasing the acrylamide to acrylate ratio did not change the expansion factors appreciably at a given crosslinker concentration, suggesting that the swelling effect of acrylate saturates at high concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The swelling effect of acrylate saturates at high concentrations.
source: Increasing the acrylamide to acrylate ratio did not change the expansion factors appreciably at a given crosslinker concentration, suggesting that the swelling effect of acrylate saturates at high concentrations.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that changing acrylate concentration did not affect expansion.

claim: At the maximum expansion factor of ~10, the deformation behavior of family D was comparable to family C.
source: At the maximum expansion factor of ~10, the deformation behavior was comparable to family C.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The authors chose to proceed with family D due to its lower acrylate content.
source: We chose to proceed with family D due to its lower acrylate content.
evidence: This explains the rationale for selecting family D.

claim: An elevated gelation temperature of 50°C (family E) was tested in an attempt to increase the initiation rate without introducing premature gelation.
source: We further tested an elevated gelation temperature of 50°C (family E) in an attempt to increase the initiation rate without introducing premature gelation as seen in recipe family B.
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale for family E.

claim: Compared to family D, the expansion factors of family E were around 15% higher at 100 µg/mL (6×) and 300 µg/mL crosslinker (9×).
source: Compared to family D, the expansion factors were around 15% higher at 100 µg/mL (6×) and 300 µg/mL crosslinker (9×), but gelation failed at lower concentrations, leaving family D as the family with a higher maximum expansion factor (i.e., 10× at 30 µg/mL bis).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Gelation failed at lower crosslinker concentrations in family E, leaving family D as the family with a higher maximum expansion factor.
source: Compared to family D, the expansion factors were around 15% higher at 100 µg/mL (6×) and 300 µg/mL crosslinker (9×), but gelation failed at lower concentrations, leaving family D as the family with a higher maximum expansion factor (i.e., 10× at 30 µg/mL bis).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The deformation versus expansion curve for family E was similar to the other high-monomer recipe families.
source: The deformation versus expansion curve for family E was similar to the other high-monomer recipe families (Figure 1D, green), but was found to be sensitive to processing details, such as the gelation chamber construction and placement within the incubator.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Family E was found to be sensitive to processing details, such as the gelation chamber construction and placement within the incubator.
source: The deformation versus expansion curve for family E was similar to the other high-monomer recipe families (Figure 1D, green), but was found to be sensitive to processing details, such as the gelation chamber construction and placement within the incubator.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Premature gelation prior to equilibrating at the higher temperature reduces the replicability of recipe family E.
source: This suggests that premature gelation prior to equilibrating at the higher temperature reduces the replicability of this recipe family.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed sensitivity to processing details.

claim: Family B displayed the lowest deformation index for a given expansion factor among all five recipe families.
source: Considering all five recipe families, family B (high acrylate and high APS/TEMED) displayed the lowest deformation index for a given expansion factor.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Family D displayed similar mechanical performance to family B, with the deformation index remaining well within the acceptable range for expansion factors up to 10.
source: Family D (high acrylamide and low APS/TEMED) displayed similar performance, with the deformation index remaining well within the acceptable range for expansion factors up to 10.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: High-expanding (>8×) gels from the standard ExM family (A) were extremely prone to fragmentation.
source: In handling high-expanding (>8×) gels from all recipe families, we found that while those from the standard ExM family (A) were extremely prone to fragmentation, those from any of the high-monomer families could be handled more easily (and even dropped from a height of several feet) without breaking.
evidence: This is an observation from handling the gels.

claim: High-expanding gels from any of the high-monomer families could be handled more easily and even dropped from a height of several feet without breaking.
source: In handling high-expanding (>8×) gels from all recipe families, we found that while those from the standard ExM family (A) were extremely prone to fragmentation, those from any of the high-monomer families could be handled more easily (and even dropped from a height of several feet) without breaking.
evidence: This is an observation from handling the gels.

claim: The reduced initiator concentration of family D results in a slower and more controlled polymerization rate.
source: Because the reduced initiator concentration of family D results in a slower and more controlled polymerization rate, and because we preferred a lower acrylate content, we chose this recipe family to proceed to biological specimen expansion.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of polymerization kinetics.

claim: The exact expansion factor varied for different specimens and gelation chamber geometries but could readily be adjusted by fine-tuning the crosslinker concentration.
source: We found that the exact expansion factor varied for different specimens and gelation chamber geometries but could readily be adjusted by fine-tuning the crosslinker concentration.
evidence: This is an observation from applying the method to biological samples.

claim: Users should test gels with a range of crosslinker concentrations between 30 and 100 µg/mL to find a suitable recipe for their specimen preparation.
source: We thus recommend that users test gels with a range of crosslinker concentrations between 30 and 100 µg/mL to find a suitable recipe for their specimen preparation.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed variability.

claim: In electron microscopy, nonspecific stains for proteins and membranes are commonly used to provide structural detail at high spatial resolution.
source: In electron microscopy, nonspecific stains for proteins and membranes are commonly used to provide structural detail at high spatial resolution.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of electron microscopy techniques.

claim: The use of nonspecific NHS ester protein stains and other small-molecule probes has recently been combined with ExM.
source: Recently, the use of nonspecific NHS ester protein stains and other small-molecule probes has been combined with ExM (M'Saad and Bewersdorf, 2020; Mao et al., 2020; Sim et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to M'Saad and Bewersdorf, 2020; Mao et al., 2020; Sim et al., 2021; and Yu et al., 2020.

claim: Expansion allows visualization of intracellular detail in densely stained samples, which would otherwise be too crowded to lead to meaningful contrast.
source: Expansion allows visualization of intracellular detail in such densely stained samples, which would otherwise be too crowded to lead to meaningful contrast.
evidence: This is an inference about the benefit of expansion for dense staining.

claim: TREx reaches single-step expansion factors at which small-molecule stains are expected to be useful.
source: Because TREx reaches single-step expansion factors at which small-molecule stains are expected to be useful, we set out to explore this idea further.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential applications of TREx.

claim: BODIPY-FL NHS was applied after expansion with TREx to demonstrate total protein distribution in thick (100 µm) slices of mouse brain cortex.
source: We applied the inexpensive, green-emitting dye BODIPY-FL NHS (total protein stain; see Materials and methods) after expansion with TREx to demonstrate total protein distribution in thick (100 µm) slices of mouse brain cortex (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The neuropil region outside the cell somas contained a rich profusion of fibers and structures visible in sharp relief.
source: The neuropil region outside the cell somas contained a rich profusion of fibers and structures visible in sharp relief.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The nucleus of each cell was easily identified, with especially strong staining in nucleoli-like structures.
source: The nucleus of each cell was easily identified, with especially strong staining in nucleoli-like structures.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The nuclear envelope could be identified, with particularly dense total protein stain on the side facing the nucleus.
source: Surrounding each nucleus, the nuclear envelope could be identified, with particularly dense total protein stain on the side facing the nucleus.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The nuclear envelope was punctuated by heavily stained spots that span the envelope, consistent with nuclear pore complexes (NPCs).
source: The nuclear envelope was punctuated by heavily stained spots that span the envelope, consistent with nuclear pore complexes (NPCs; Figure 2A, inset).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2A, with inference about the identity of the structures.

claim: Within the cytosol, several organelles were marked by either heavy inner staining with a dim border or weak inner staining.
source: Within the cytosol, several organelles were marked by either heavy inner staining with a dim border or weak inner staining.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The authors attempted to optimize protein retention by reducing both protein anchoring and proteolysis compared with the original ExM.
source: We attempted to optimize protein retention, according to the total protein stain intensity, by reducing both protein anchoring and proteolysis compared with the original ExM.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: A range of anchoring strengths was tested by varying the concentration of the acryloyl-X SE (AcX) anchoring molecule applied prior to gelation.
source: We tested a range of anchoring strengths by varying the concentration of the acryloyl-X SE (AcX) anchoring molecule applied prior to gelation.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The protease-free treatment enabled greater protein retention but at the cost of incomplete expansion.
source: The protease-free treatment enabled greater protein retention but at the cost of incomplete expansion.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Incomplete expansion from protease-free treatment could be offset through reduced AcX concentration.
source: This could be offset through reduced AcX concentration, though this was not clearly superior to high AcX followed by proteolysis, indicating a general tradeoff between protein retention and gel expansion (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is a general tradeoff between protein retention and gel expansion.
source: This could be offset through reduced AcX concentration, though this was not clearly superior to high AcX followed by proteolysis, indicating a general tradeoff between protein retention and gel expansion (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The authors chose a hybrid approach with moderate AcX anchoring and low-concentration proteinase K digestion followed by high-temperature denaturation to proceed.
source: We chose a hybrid approach with moderate AcX anchoring and low-concentration proteinase K digestion followed by high-temperature denaturation to proceed.
evidence: This describes the chosen experimental protocol.

claim: Antibodies applied to the tissue using a standard immunofluorescence procedure before embedding were retained in the TREx gel.
source: We next tested whether antibodies, applied to the tissue using a standard immunofluorescence procedure before embedding, were also retained in the TREx gel.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Numerous putative excitatory synapses were observed at high density, with clearly separated Bassoon and Homer pre- and postsynaptic staining.
source: Numerous putative excitatory synapses were observed at high density, with clearly separated Bassoon and Homer pre- and postsynaptic staining (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: TREx allowed quantification of the separation of Bassoon and Homer in 3D, regardless of the angle of the synapse with respect to the imaging plane.
source: Because of the excellent axial resolution, TREx allowed us to quantify the separation of Bassoon and Homer in 3D, regardless of the angle of the synapse with respect to the imaging plane (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The average separation of Bassoon and Homer was 1.17 µm ± 0.52 µm (mean ± SD, 583 synapses).
source: We found an average separation of 1.17 µm ± 0.52 µm (mean ± SD, 583 synapses), which, when corrected for expansion, is consistent with previous reports in cultured neurons that estimated the synapse separation between 90 and 130 nm (Glebov et al., 2016; Wiesner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The measured Bassoon-Homer separation, when corrected for expansion, is consistent with previous reports in cultured neurons that estimated the synapse separation between 90 and 130 nm.
source: We found an average separation of 1.17 µm ± 0.52 µm (mean ± SD, 583 synapses), which, when corrected for expansion, is consistent with previous reports in cultured neurons that estimated the synapse separation between 90 and 130 nm (Glebov et al., 2016; Wiesner et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glebov et al., 2016 and Wiesner et al., 2020, and comparison with the measured data.

claim: VGAT had a more extended staining pattern compared to Bassoon and Homer, consistent with the known distribution of synaptic vesicles throughout presynaptic boutons.
source: Compared with Bassoon and Homer, VGAT had a more extended staining pattern, consistent with the known distribution of synaptic vesicles throughout presynaptic boutons.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2C, with inference based on known biology.

claim: Elaborately shaped compartments with dense VGAT staining were seen with multiple synaptic release sites marked by Bassoon.
source: Elaborately shaped compartments with dense VGAT staining were seen with multiple synaptic release sites marked by Bassoon (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Synaptic release sites with VGAT staining were not paired with the excitatory postsynaptic marker Homer.
source: As expected, these release sites were not paired with the excitatory postsynaptic marker Homer.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2C, consistent with known biology.

claim: Spatial correlation was observed in excitatory synapses between Homer and Bassoon, reflecting the transsynaptic alignment reported previously.
source: In addition, spatial correlation was observed in excitatory synapses between Homer and Bassoon, reflecting the transsynaptic alignment reported previously (Hruska et al., 2018; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, supported by citation to Hruska et al., 2018.

claim: TREx demonstrates the ability to preserve correct synaptic staining while enabling sub-diffraction limited imaging of large tissue sections.
source: These results demonstrate the ability of TREx to preserve correct synaptic staining while enabling sub-diffraction limited imaging of large tissue sections.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Increasing the expansion factor from 4 to 10× could result in greater sensitivity of the expansion factor to local variation, for example, in protein dense complexes, resulting in less uniform expansion.
source: Increasing the expansion factor from 4 to 10× could result in greater sensitivity of the expansion factor to local variation, for example, in protein dense complexes, resulting in less uniform expansion.
evidence: This is speculation about potential issues with higher expansion factors.

claim: The authors explored the nanoscale isotropy of TREx by imaging NPCs, which have a highly stereotyped and well-characterized structure.
source: To examine this, we explored the nanoscale isotropy of TREx by imaging NPCs, which have a highly stereotyped and well-characterized structure.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: The NPC constituent protein nucleoporin 96 (NUP96) appears in a ring structure with a 107 nm diameter.
source: The NPC constituent protein nucleoporin 96 (NUP96) appears in a ring structure with a 107 nm diameter (Thevathasan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Thevathasan et al., 2019.

claim: NPCs have recently been explored as a reference structure for super-resolution microscopy methods, including ExM in combination with other super-resolution methods.
source: NPCs have recently been explored as a reference structure for super-resolution microscopy methods, including ExM in combination with other super-resolution methods (Pesce et al., 2019; Thevathasan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pesce et al., 2019 and Thevathasan et al., 2019.

claim: For the conventional 4–5× expansion approach, the diameter of the NPC was 14–29% smaller than expected from the macroscopic expansion of the gel.
source: For the conventional 4–5× expansion approach, this revealed that the diameter of the NPC was 14–29% smaller than expected from the macroscopic expansion of the gel.
evidence: This is based on prior work, likely from the cited references.

claim: After expansion with TREx, individual NPCs were uniformly retained and clearly visible using diffraction-limited confocal microscopy.
source: After expansion with TREx, individual NPCs were uniformly retained and clearly visible using diffraction-limited confocal microscopy (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An antibody against NUP153 demonstrated individual NPCs but with less complete NPC coverage compared with the antibody stain against the NUP96-GFP tag.
source: An antibody against NUP153 similarly demonstrated individual NPCs but with less complete NPC coverage compared with the antibody stain against the NUP96-GFP tag (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The macroscopic gel expansion factor was 9.5×.
source: The macroscopic gel expansion factor was 9.5×, suggesting an expected NPC size after expansion of 107 nm × 9.5 = 1.02 µm.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experiment.

claim: The expected NPC size after 9.5× expansion is 1.02 µm.
source: The macroscopic gel expansion factor was 9.5×, suggesting an expected NPC size after expansion of 107 nm × 9.5 = 1.02 µm.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the known NPC size and measured expansion factor.

claim: The size of NPCs after expansion was 939 nm ± 90 nm (mean ± SD) based on 60 NPCs from three nonadjacent cells.
source: We used a semi-automated approach to determining the diameter of 60 NPCs randomly chosen from three nonadjacent cells and found the size after expansion to be 939 nm ± 90 nm (mean ± SD) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The measured NPC size is about 8% smaller than expected based on the macroscopic expansion of the gel.
source: This is about 8% smaller than expected based on the macroscopic expansion of the gel and implies a local expansion factor of 8.8×, or 92% of the expected 9.5×.
evidence: This is a calculation comparing the measured and expected NPC sizes.

claim: The local expansion factor of NPCs is 8.8×, or 92% of the expected 9.5×.
source: This is about 8% smaller than expected based on the macroscopic expansion of the gel and implies a local expansion factor of 8.8×, or 92% of the expected 9.5×.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured NPC size.

claim: TREx offers more uniform local expansion compared to conventional ExM.
source: These data indicate that TREx offers more uniform local expansion compared to conventional ExM.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing the 8% discrepancy in TREx to the 14-29% discrepancy in conventional ExM.

claim: Other reference structures for super-resolution microscopy include microtubules and clathrin-coated pits (CCPs), which have been extensively studied with various modalities including ExM.
source: Other reference structures for super-resolution microscopy include microtubules and clathrin-coated pits (CCPs), which have been extensively studied with various modalities including ExM (Bates et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bates et al., 2007 and Chen et al., 2015.

claim: The average diameter of CCPs was 1.16 ± 0.2 µm (mean ± SD).
source: We found an average diameter of 1.16 ± 0.2 µm (mean ± SD), which, corrected for 10-fold expansion, is consistent with previously reported values (Chen et al., 2015; Jones et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The measured CCP diameter, corrected for 10-fold expansion, is consistent with previously reported values.
source: We found an average diameter of 1.16 ± 0.2 µm (mean ± SD), which, corrected for 10-fold expansion, is consistent with previously reported values (Chen et al., 2015; Jones et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Jones et al., 2011, and comparison with the measured data.

claim: In samples with sufficiently high labeling densities, the stereotyped M-profile across peripheral microtubules in COS7 cells could be resolved, indicative of the hollow structure of microtubules.
source: In samples with sufficiently high labeling densities (e.g., the periphery of COS7 cells), we could furthermore resolve the stereotyped M-profile across peripheral microtubules in COS7 cells, indicative of the hollow structure of microtubules.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: For microtubules stained with primary and secondary antibodies, a 450-nm peak-to-peak distance after expansion was observed.
source: As expected for microtubules stained with primary and secondary antibodies (Mikhaylova et al., 2015), we observed a 450-nm peak-to-peak distance after expansion (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a measurement from the data shown in Figure 3G, supported by citation to Mikhaylova et al., 2015.

claim: The authors quantified the measurement error introduced by nonuniform expansion by comparing antibody-stained microtubules imaged before expansion with 3D gSTED versus after expansion with confocal microscopy.
source: Next, we quantified the measurement error introduced by nonuniform expansion by comparing antibody-stained microtubules imaged before expansion with 3D gSTED versus after expansion with confocal microscopy (Figure 3H–J), as described previously (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach, supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: For a large tiled acquisition of 42 fields of view from one gel (~650 × 750 µm after expansion), the measurement error was found to be a constant fraction (3.2% ± 1.7%) of the measurement length.
source: For a large tiled acquisition of 42 fields of view from one gel (~650 × 750 µm after expansion), the measurement error was found to be a constant fraction (3.2% ± 1.7%) of the measurement length (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The similarity transform was used to calculate the overall expansion factor of the entire imaged area, which was found to be 9.4×.
source: We used the similarity transform to calculate the overall expansion factor of the entire imaged area and found it to be 9.4×, consistent with the expansion expected for the whole gel.
evidence: This is a measurement from the analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The measured expansion factor of 9.4× is consistent with the expansion expected for the whole gel.
source: We used the similarity transform to calculate the overall expansion factor of the entire imaged area and found it to be 9.4×, consistent with the expansion expected for the whole gel.
evidence: This is a comparison of the measured expansion factor with the expected value.

claim: TREx enables uniform single-step, 10-fold expansion that retains structural detail over large distances, in both cultured cells and thick tissue slices, with similar performance compared with the original 4× ExM.
source: Together, these data show that TREx enables uniform single-step, 10-fold expansion that retains structural detail over large distances, in both cultured cells and thick tissue slices, with similar performance compared with the original 4× ExM.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: A custom-synthesized membrane probe compatible with the ExM process has been shown to visualize membranes in fixed brain tissue.
source: For membranes, a custom-synthesized membrane probe compatible with the ExM process has been shown to visualize membranes in fixed brain tissue (Karagiannis et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Karagiannis et al., 2019.

claim: The custom membrane probe relies on a peptide-modified lipid tail that intercalates in target membranes and provides opportunities for anchoring to the gel through D-lysines in its peptide sequence.
source: This probe relies on a peptide-modified lipid tail that intercalates in target membranes and provides opportunities for anchoring to the gel through D-lysines in its peptide sequence.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the custom probe based on citation to Karagiannis et al., 2019.

claim: The authors asked whether the commercially available membrane-binding probe mCLING could also be used for membrane staining and gel anchoring.
source: We asked whether the commercially available membrane-binding probe mCLING could also be used for membrane staining and gel anchoring.
evidence: This describes the research question.

claim: mCLING has been developed as a fixable endocytosis marker consisting of a fluorophore and a short polypeptide group with one cysteine and seven lysines coupled to a palmitoyl membrane anchor.
source: mCLING has been developed as a fixable endocytosis marker consisting of a fluorophore and a short polypeptide group with one cysteine and seven lysines coupled to a palmitoyl membrane anchor (Revelo and Rizzoli, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Revelo and Rizzoli, 2016.

claim: Due to the presence of multiple lysines, mCLING would be compatible with standard ExM anchoring through AcX.
source: Due to the presence of multiple lysines, we hypothesized that mCLING would be compatible with standard ExM anchoring through AcX.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the chemical structure of mCLING.

claim: The standard protocol for mCLING delivery relies on active endocytosis in living cells.
source: While the standard protocol for mCLING delivery relies on active endocytosis in living cells, we tested whether mCLING would stain intracellular membranes more uniformly when added to fixed cells, which would have the added benefit of not perturbing intracellular membrane trafficking by long incubation in live cells.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the standard mCLING protocol.

claim: The authors tested whether mCLING would stain intracellular membranes more uniformly when added to fixed cells.
source: While the standard protocol for mCLING delivery relies on active endocytosis in living cells, we tested whether mCLING would stain intracellular membranes more uniformly when added to fixed cells, which would have the added benefit of not perturbing intracellular membrane trafficking by long incubation in live cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: Adding mCLING to fixed cells would have the added benefit of not perturbing intracellular membrane trafficking by long incubation in live cells.
source: While the standard protocol for mCLING delivery relies on active endocytosis in living cells, we tested whether mCLING would stain intracellular membranes more uniformly when added to fixed cells, which would have the added benefit of not perturbing intracellular membrane trafficking by long incubation in live cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the modified protocol.

claim: mCLING efficiently intercalates in both the plasma membrane and internal organelles and is retained following standard anchoring procedure.
source: We found that mCLING efficiently intercalates in both the plasma membrane and internal organelles and is retained following our standard anchoring procedure (Figure 4A, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: By carefully rendering the imaged volumes, both the ruffled morphology of the plasma membrane on top of the flattened part of the cell and the organelle clustering typical of activated T cells could be visualized with one probe.
source: By carefully rendering the imaged volumes, we could, with one probe, both appreciate the ruffled morphology of the plasma membrane on top of the flattened part of the cell and visualize the organelle clustering typical of activated T cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Different organelles could be clearly identified based on mCLING, suggesting that it could be used for automated segmentation of organelles.
source: As in electron microscopy, where distinct morphologies are used to identify organelles, we could clearly identify different organelles based on mCLING, suggesting that it could be used for automated segmentation of organelles.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data with inference about potential applications.

claim: Mitochondria could be readily segmented using a trainable Weka segmentation algorithm.
source: Indeed, we found that mitochondria could be readily segmented using a trainable Weka segmentation algorithm (Figure 4B; Arganda-Carreras et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B, supported by citation to Arganda-Carreras et al., 2017.

claim: TREx allows sufficient single-step expansion to resolve individual mitochondrial cristae.
source: While the resolution of subcellular structures is limited by the density of mCLING moieties in the membrane, the efficiency of crosslinking to the gel, and the maximum expansion factor, we found that TREx allows sufficient single-step expansion to resolve individual mitochondrial cristae (Figure 4C), which are known to be as closely spaced as 70 nm (Stephan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 4C, supported by citation to Stephan et al., 2019.

claim: Mitochondrial cristae are known to be as closely spaced as 70 nm.
source: While the resolution of subcellular structures is limited by the density of mCLING moieties in the membrane, the efficiency of crosslinking to the gel, and the maximum expansion factor, we found that TREx allows sufficient single-step expansion to resolve individual mitochondrial cristae (Figure 4C), which are known to be as closely spaced as 70 nm (Stephan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stephan et al., 2019.

claim: mCLING is membrane impermeable in live cells due to multiple positively charged amino groups.
source: Although mCLING is membrane impermeable in live cells (due to multiple positively charged amino groups), it readily stained fixed and unpermeabilized cells following extended incubation.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of mCLING properties.

claim: mCLING readily stained fixed and unpermeabilized cells following extended incubation.
source: Although mCLING is membrane impermeable in live cells (due to multiple positively charged amino groups), it readily stained fixed and unpermeabilized cells following extended incubation.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: The approach of adding mCLING to fixed cells does not require labeling live cells and is expected to reduce differences in uptake efficiency between intracellular compartments.
source: Because this approach does not require labeling live cells and is expected to reduce differences in uptake efficiency between intracellular compartments, we used this approach in all subsequent experiments.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the modified protocol.

claim: Using TREx, the entire Caco-2 monolayer could be expanded and membranes visualized using mCLING.
source: Using TREx, we could expand the entire monolayer and visualize membranes using mCLING (Figure 4D–H, Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 4D-H.

claim: The advantage of optical, volumetric imaging is that one dataset can be easily rendered in several ways, either resembling scanning electron microscopy to highlight volumetric surface morphology or transmission electron microscopy to explore single planes in more detail.
source: The advantage of optical, volumetric imaging is underscored by the fact that we can easily render one dataset in several ways, either resembling scanning electron microscopy to highlight volumetric surface morphology (Figure 4D) or transmission electron microscopy to explore single planes in more detail (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The elaborate interdigitated cell-cell junctions in Caco-2 cells could be resolved, which could previously only be clearly appreciated using electron microscopy.
source: For example, we were able to resolve the elaborate interdigitated cell-cell junctions that could previously only be clearly appreciated using electron microscopy (Drenckhahn and Franz, 1986), as well as resolve individual microvilli as hollow membrane protrusions within the dense brush border.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data, supported by citation to Drenckhahn and Franz, 1986.

claim: Individual microvilli could be resolved as hollow membrane protrusions within the dense brush border.
source: For example, we were able to resolve the elaborate interdigitated cell-cell junctions that could previously only be clearly appreciated using electron microscopy (Drenckhahn and Franz, 1986), as well as resolve individual microvilli as hollow membrane protrusions within the dense brush border.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Dense brush borders of differentiated cells could only be resolved in the 10× gel, not in the 4.5× gel.
source: When the 10× and 4.5× expanded gels were imaged, dense brush borders of differentiated cells could only be resolved in the 10× gel (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The average diameter of individual microvilli was 1.08 ± 0.16 µm (n = 12,339 from 12 cells, N = 3).
source: Indeed, we found an average diameter of 1.08 ± 0.16 µm (n = 12,339 from 12 cells, N = 3), which, corrected for an expansion factor of 10, is within 8% of the value from electron microscopy.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Microvilli have been thoroughly characterized with EM with a diameter of ~100 nm.
source: To validate the expansion factor, we quantified the diameter of individual microvilli as these have been thoroughly characterized with EM with a diameter of ~100 nm (Crawley et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Crawley et al., 2014.

claim: The measured microvilli diameter, corrected for an expansion factor of 10, is within 8% of the value from electron microscopy.
source: Indeed, we found an average diameter of 1.08 ± 0.16 µm (n = 12,339 from 12 cells, N = 3), which, corrected for an expansion factor of 10, is within 8% of the value from electron microscopy.
evidence: This is a comparison of the measured data with literature values.

claim: TREx is robust in expanding multiple cell types.
source: Together, these data illustrate the robustness of TREx in expanding multiple cell types and show how the increased expansion factor combined with a commercially available membrane stain provides rapid volumetric insights into the elaborate membranous architecture of cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The increased expansion factor of TREx combined with a commercially available membrane stain provides rapid volumetric insights into the elaborate membranous architecture of cells.
source: Together, these data illustrate the robustness of TREx in expanding multiple cell types and show how the increased expansion factor combined with a commercially available membrane stain provides rapid volumetric insights into the elaborate membranous architecture of cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Previously, ExM was used to study the three-dimensional organization of microtubules in neurons and T cells.
source: Previously, we used ExM to study the three-dimensional organization of microtubules in neurons and T cells (Hooikaas et al., 2020; Jurriens et al., 2021; Katrukha et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hooikaas et al., 2020; Jurriens et al., 2021; and Katrukha et al., 2021.

claim: In previous ExM experiments, cells were typically pre-extracted with detergent and glutaraldehyde to reduce background, followed by paraformaldehyde fixation.
source: In these experiments, cells were typically pre-extracted with detergent and glutaraldehyde to reduce background, followed by paraformaldehyde fixation (Tas et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tas et al., 2017.

claim: The increased expansion of TREx would dilute the soluble tubulin background, resulting in a relative boost in signal over background and eliminating the need for pre-extraction.
source: We reasoned that the increased expansion of TREx would dilute the soluble tubulin background, resulting in a relative boost in signal over background and eliminating the need for pre-extraction to enable high-resolution imaging of microtubules in combination with membranes.
evidence: This is an inference about the benefits of higher expansion.

claim: Expanded cells retained high-quality anti-tubulin antibody signal exhibiting high contrast relative to the cytosolic background.
source: Expanded cells retained high-quality anti-tubulin antibody signal exhibiting high contrast relative to the cytosolic background.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increased detail in both mCLING and tubulin stains was observed after expansion compared to before expansion.
source: We also observed increased detail in both mCLING and tubulin stains after expansion compared to before expansion, which was particularly apparent with side views of the same cell (Figure 5A, far right).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The average tubule diameter of ER stained with mCLING was 0.79 ± 0.1 µm.
source: Indeed, we observed an average tubule diameter of 0.79 ± 0.1 µm for mCLING, which, corrected for 10-fold expansion, is consistent with the previously published range of 60–100 nm (Shibata et al., 2009; Shibata et al., 2006), while the anti-GFP signal from the same tubules is broadened to an average diameter of 0.93 ± 0.1 µm.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The measured ER tubule diameter with mCLING, corrected for 10-fold expansion, is consistent with the previously published range of 60–100 nm.
source: Indeed, we observed an average tubule diameter of 0.79 ± 0.1 µm for mCLING, which, corrected for 10-fold expansion, is consistent with the previously published range of 60–100 nm (Shibata et al., 2009; Shibata et al., 2006), while the anti-GFP signal from the same tubules is broadened to an average diameter of 0.93 ± 0.1 µm.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shibata et al., 2009 and Shibata et al., 2006, and comparison with the measured data.

claim: The anti-GFP signal from ER tubules is broadened to an average diameter of 0.93 ± 0.1 µm.
source: Indeed, we observed an average tubule diameter of 0.79 ± 0.1 µm for mCLING, which, corrected for 10-fold expansion, is consistent with the previously published range of 60–100 nm (Shibata et al., 2009; Shibata et al., 2006), while the anti-GFP signal from the same tubules is broadened to an average diameter of 0.93 ± 0.1 µm.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The broadening of apparent ER tubule width is due to antibody linkage error.
source: Indeed, we observed an average tubule diameter of 0.79 ± 0.1 µm for mCLING, which, corrected for 10-fold expansion, is consistent with the previously published range of 60–100 nm (Shibata et al., 2009; Shibata et al., 2006), while the anti-GFP signal from the same tubules is broadened to an average diameter of 0.93 ± 0.1 µm.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of mCLING and anti-GFP measurements.

claim: Within the same dataset, the interplay between microtubules and ER in three dimensions could be resolved.
source: Within the same dataset, the interplay between microtubules and ER (Figure 5D) in three dimensions could be resolved, which revealed how other membranous organelles were connected to both structures (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: TREx facilitates high-resolution three-dimensional mapping of specific cytoskeletal and membranous structures in combination with markers that provide ultrastructural context.
source: Thus, TREx facilitates high-resolution three-dimensional mapping of specific cytoskeletal and membranous structures in combination with markers that provide ultrastructural context.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The authors tested whether TREx using general membrane stains could be combined with general protein stains and/or antibody stains.
source: Finally, we tested whether TREx using general membrane stains could be combined with general protein stains and/or antibody stains.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: Secondary antibodies that had been used to stain GFP before gelation withstood the high-temperature denaturing disruption step.
source: We found that secondary antibodies that had been used to stain GFP before gelation withstood this disruption step.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: A clear degree of overlap was observed between mCLING and NHS, especially in the dense perinuclear region.
source: We observed a clear degree of overlap between mCLING and NHS, especially in the dense perinuclear region, but we could also identify distinct features of each stain (Figure 5E, bottom).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Distinct features of mCLING and NHS stains could be identified.
source: We observed a clear degree of overlap between mCLING and NHS, especially in the dense perinuclear region, but we could also identify distinct features of each stain (Figure 5E, bottom).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: General stains for membranes and proteins can be combined with antibody-based labeling to reveal specific proteins in their ultrastructural context.
source: These results demonstrate that general stains for membranes and proteins can be combined with antibody-based labeling to reveal specific proteins in their ultrastructural context.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: TREx was developed to expand biological specimens 10-fold in a single round of expansion, without specialized equipment or procedures.
source: We developed TREx in order to expand biological specimens 10-fold in a single round of expansion, without specialized equipment or procedures.
evidence: This is a summary of the main achievement of the work.

claim: A framework was established for assessing gel recipes operating near the apparent limit of single-round expansion.
source: In developing this method, we established a framework for assessing gel recipes operating near this apparent limit of single-round expansion.
evidence: This describes the methodological contribution of the work.

claim: The mechanical performance of gel recipes varies smoothly with changes in crosslinker.
source: We found that the mechanical performance of gel recipes, that is, resistance to deformation versus gel expansion factor, varies smoothly with changes in crosslinker.
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic exploration shown in Figure 1.

claim: For all high-monomer (~3 molar total acrylamide and acrylate) gel recipe families, the relation between expansion factor and crosslinker concentration fell close to a common curve.
source: For all high-monomer (~3 molar total acrylamide and acrylate) gel recipe families, the relation between expansion factor and crosslinker concentration fell close to a common curve.
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic exploration shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The high radical initiation rate of family B enabled gelation without the inclusion of a crosslinker.
source: The high radical initiation rate of family B enabled gelation without the inclusion of a crosslinker, suggesting that side reactions and polymer entanglement in these conditions create sufficient network crosslinks to form a gel.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Side reactions and polymer entanglement in family B conditions create sufficient network crosslinks to form a gel.
source: The high radical initiation rate of family B enabled gelation without the inclusion of a crosslinker, suggesting that side reactions and polymer entanglement in these conditions create sufficient network crosslinks to form a gel.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that gels form without added crosslinker.

claim: Gel deformation measurements plotted versus expansion factor show high-monomer recipe families falling close to a common curve.
source: Gel deformation measurements plotted versus expansion factor, though less precise, also show high-monomer recipe families falling close to a common curve.
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic exploration shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Compared to the high-monomer families, the original ExM recipe family is less resistant to deformation for a given expansion factor.
source: Compared to the high-monomer families, the original ExM recipe family is less resistant to deformation for a given expansion factor and expands more for a given crosslinker concentration.
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic exploration shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The original ExM recipe family expands more for a given crosslinker concentration compared to high-monomer families.
source: Compared to the high-monomer families, the original ExM recipe family is less resistant to deformation for a given expansion factor and expands more for a given crosslinker concentration.
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic exploration shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The factor determining gel properties is the density of effective crosslinks formed between neighboring polymer chains in the gel, not crosslinker concentration in the gel recipe per se.
source: The factor determining gel properties is not crosslinker concentration in the gel recipe per se, but rather the density of effective crosslinks formed between neighboring polymer chains in the gel.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed differences between recipe families.

claim: The original, low-monomer recipe less efficiently incorporates crosslinker molecules as network crosslinks.
source: This suggests that the original, low-monomer recipe less efficiently incorporates crosslinker molecules as network crosslinks.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed differences in expansion and deformation behavior.

claim: The lower rate of chain extension in the original recipe may allow incorporated crosslinker molecules to be re-reacted by the same polymer chain before they can react with neighboring polymers.
source: This may be because the resulting lower rate of chain extension allows incorporated crosslinker molecules to be re-reacted by the same polymer chain before they can react with neighboring polymers.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed differences.

claim: It has been shown that increasing the monomer content is required to maintain nanoscale isotropy using centrioles as a convenient standard reference structure.
source: While the expansion factor of the original ExM recipe can be tuned by varying the crosslinker concentration, it has been shown that increasing the monomer content is required to maintain nanoscale isotropy using centrioles as a convenient standard reference structure (Gambarotto et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gambarotto et al., 2019.

claim: TREx has been rapidly adopted by other labs.
source: By systematically exploring the ExM recipe space, we established a novel recipe using standard ExM reagents that has been rapidly adopted by other labs.
evidence: This is supported by the citations to other work using TREx mentioned in the Discussion.

claim: TREx has been successfully applied in cultured neurons.
source: This robustness is further demonstrated by its adoption in other biological systems (Gros et al., 2021) including in cultured neurons (Ozkan et al., 2021) and primary cultured human cells (Nijenhuis et al., 2021), and by its superior mechanical properties as measured by traditional materials characterization methods (Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ozkan et al., 2021.

claim: TREx has been successfully applied in primary cultured human cells.
source: This robustness is further demonstrated by its adoption in other biological systems (Gros et al., 2021) including in cultured neurons (Ozkan et al., 2021) and primary cultured human cells (Nijenhuis et al., 2021), and by its superior mechanical properties as measured by traditional materials characterization methods (Chen et al., 2021).
